items.stem: What is the fundamental scientific requirement for mechanical work to be done on an object by an applied force?
items.answer: Work is scientifically defined as the product of the force applied to an object and its displacement in the direction of that force. If an object does not move despite heavy force, the displacement is zero, resulting in zero work. This fundamental physics concept clearly differentiates everyday effort from actual mechanical work performed on physical objects.

options.label: A
options.text: The object must be stationary while the heavy force is applied.

options.label: B
options.text: The object must gain excessive mass during the force application.

options.label: C
options.text: The object must be displaced along the direction of the applied force.

options.label: D
options.text: The object must be displaced completely perpendicular to the applied force.

items.stem: A student applies a massive push force against a solid, unmoving brick wall for several minutes until physically exhausted. How much scientific work is done on the wall?

options.label: A
options.text: Positive work, because significant muscular effort was continuously exerted.

options.label: B
options.text: Negative work, because the wall pushed back with an equal opposite force.

options.label: C
options.text: Infinite work, because the wall is highly resistant to any motion.

options.label: D
options.text: Zero work, because the wall did not physically displace from its position.

items.stem: Why do you push an object closer to scissors (fulcrum) when you want to cut an object which is hard?
items.answer: Scissors are levers, and placing a hard object closer to the pivot point (fulcrum) effectively shortens the load arm. Since mechanical advantage is calculated as the effort arm divided by the load arm, a shorter load arm increases the mechanical advantage. This means the same squeezing force from your hand results in a much greater cutting force on the object, making it easier to cut tough materials.

items.stem: Throughout history, many designs of perpetual machines (using wheels, weights or magnets) have been proposed but none actually work. Why do all real machines eventually slow down and stop? Explain in terms of work and energy.
items.answer: Real machines eventually stop because it is impossible to eliminate friction and air resistance completely. As a machine’s parts move, internal forces oppose the motion, meaning the machine must constantly do work against friction. This work converts the useful mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal energy (heat) and sound. Without an external energy source to replace this lost mechanical energy, the machine will run out of kinetic energy and stop. NCER T Exercis
